Unfortunately, conventional approaches suffer from low resolution, distorted details, and lack of adaptability to different camera angles. Our novel approach, DiffDreamer, leverages conditional diffusion models to generate high-quality, detailed 3D single-view productions. By utilizing coarse inputs and enhancing the generative process with control mechanisms, DiffDreamer produces superior results compared to previous methods. The results show that DiffDreamer outperforms existing techniques in multiple aspects, including detailed production quality, consistency, and resistance to input errors. The code behind DiffDreamer can be found at https://github.com/automl/DiffDreamer.

Effective predictive tools are essential in highly dynamic network systems. Our approach combines a combination of data analytics techniques to improve system performance through its own experiences over time. Using a stochastic SIS model on an airline network as an example, our methodology accurately forecasts passenger movement between airports and suggests capacity adjustments based on predicted passenger volumes. Moreover, guiding capacity adjustments based on passenger flow can enhance service quality and significantly reduce prediction errors. Evaluations conducted through simulations demonstrate the integration of our data-driven strategy leads to notable enhancements over traditional feedback-controlled systems.

The behavior of a liquid layer on a thin, spinning fiber has been investigated through both numerical simulations and theoretical analysis. Theoretically, it's been discovered that the liquid layer becomes unstable due to the interaction between capillary forces and shear, resulting in the formation of droplets at specific distances. This phenomenon can be explained by considering how the shear affects the instability of the liquid layer. Moreover, the onset of droplet formation occurs earlier when the layer is thicker and the shear is more intense in thinner liquid layers. Numerical simulations have confirmed the theoretical predictions and shown that droplets form further away from the spinning end of the fiber compared to an ideal, frictionless environment. These simulations have also revealed the presence of waves propagating along the liquid layer just before droplets start to form significantly. Interestingly, the spacing of these droplets does not significantly depend on the thickness of the liquid layer once it has started to form. However, droplet formation occurs much faster in thicker liquid layers compared to thinner ones.

This study is built upon the foundation laid by Chae and Strong, who established Lipschitz Lipschitz continuity for the Hunter-Saxton equation in one spatial dimension, in Annals of Global Analysis and Geometry (to appear). Our contribution further builds on their work by adapting their approach to the modified Hunter-Saxton formula found in Armin et al.'s work in Discrete and Continuous Continuous Virtual Experiments (2019). Additionally, our proof demonstrates continuity with respect to the measure of one particle distance.

Assessing scoliosis with robotic ultrasound is more reliable than having a patient try to scan their own spine. The difference in detection accuracy between the two methods is statistically significant. When using a robot to scan the spine, specific ROIs are automatically located with high reliability, ensuring that dependability is not influenced by variations in scanning technique.

This research introduces an innovative approach to synthesizing human speech by dynamically generating word durations based on a text-based speaker profile. We present a novel statistical model for calculating word lengths as non-Gaussian distributions. This model is grounded in the median word duration and an error margin derived from a historical speech dataset, which allows for robustness against outliers. Additionally, our method supports incorporating linguistic cues from a phonetic transcription to adjust the synthetic speech tempo. We evaluate the proposed model's effectiveness through a comparison with previously established methods.

Hate speech is defined as abusive language directed towards individuals, groups, ideas, or institutions, fostering animosity, discrimination, or hatred. The proliferation of hate speech online on social media platforms is detrimental to online discourse and real-life outcomes, potentially leading to violence and disruptions in daily life. Detecting hate speech automatically through computational methods necessitates understanding how humans perceive hate, particularly highlighting hate's distinct characteristics. Existing approaches to hate speech detection primarily rely on predefined feature sets, which may overlook unique aspects of hate speech expressions. In response, this research suggests using a deep learning model to automatically extract and consider distinctive characteristics when detecting hate speech, either in the original text or through related concepts. The results of this study demonstrate notable improvements when incorporating distinctive features into the task, particularly for the English dataset. The findings also indicate the importance of distinctive features and the benefits of incorporating augmented data representations for better hate speech detection. The techniques developed in this research are expected to contribute to the development of a more effective hate speech detection system.

The rapid increase in data transfer demands is driving the necessity for high-speed wireless communication. Multiple-Input Multiple-Output technologies are becoming essential in meeting these needs, as they enable significant boosts in data transmission rates and overall system efficiency. Multiple wireless signals are sent and received simultaneously in MIMO systems, resulting in a highly complex and interdependent environment. This MIMO setting poses difficulties for extracting and sending key features, as it is challenging to preserve critical information and maintain integrity. These obstacles become even more pronounced in MIMO networks, as features are continuously transformed and adapted. Despite MIMO's numerous advantages, its application is hindered by these complexities, limiting its effectiveness and usability. Various techniques and strategies are being investigated to overcome MIMO's limitations and optimize its performance. This paper explores the underlying complexities of MIMO systems and presents potential solutions to mitigate these issues.

Historical archives containing numerous handwritten documents, such as letters and diaries, are invaluable sources for researching the history of the past. An analysis of 1,200 collections spanning 100 years reveals the significance of these archives, with each collection accompanied by detailed metadata, including the author, time period, language, and the hosting institution. A review of these collections is provided, with links to each archive, allowing researchers to explore historical writing collections within a specific time frame and geographic region.

Industrial robots are versatile tools capable of performing tasks such as precision picking and placing, welding, and grinding.  The performance of these robots heavily relies on the accuracy of their joint position positioning systems, positioned at the intersection of the shaft and link segments.  To position these systems, pre-installed proximity sensors position pressure at these critical points, allowing for position position positioning.  The monitoring and regulation of flatness (the difference between the largest and smallest diameter of a joint) become essential in maintaining position position positioning.  The effective grasp and torque distribution during object manipulation are heavily influenced by joint position positioning.  The objective of this paper is to introduce position-based control techniques for tracking the movement of industrial robots' joints, using pressure data from the proximity sensors to determine the flatness of the joint.  The proposed position-based control method is verified through a physical experiment on an ABB IRB1440 robot and the results show position-based position positioning, allowing for position-based position positioning.

A novel approach known as Multiple State Evaluation (MSE) has been developed to analyze complex medical information. It enables the comparison of various health trajectories for different groups of patients. In this study, we modified the MSE model to include an additional state representing death. Our framework compares the effectiveness of treatments by considering the complexity of patients' health states over time. In this context, we compared the impact of Medicare reimbursement policies on patients who experienced a heart attack. Our model divides patients into different health states based on specific conditions. We estimated and visualized MSE results using numerical calculations and visual aids derived from structural equation modeling. Our analysis showed that an increase in reimbursement for nursing homes significantly shortened patients' lives, but had a negligible effect on those on medical insurance, likely due to variations in lifestyle choices and socioeconomic factors.

The concept of molecular continua, where substances are modeled as fluids with complex intermolecular forces, has been proven challenging to apply due to their complex nature. However, treating these forces as body forces within fluid dynamics frameworks offers a more accurate and model-consistent approach. This method involves creating a discrete representation of the force field through a spatial quadrature, allowing for an accurate and efficient force evaluation. A specific approach is introduced here to assess the accuracy of this force discretization. It demonstrates that standard quadrature techniques, such as linear or quadratic methods, are insufficient due to the smooth but non-analytic behavior of the force field. Consequently, higher-order quadrature rules are required, specifically cubic or higher-order rules, which are typically reserved for small spatial scales. This approach is particularly beneficial for simulating phenomena involving multi-scale processes. A specific application involves the simulation of droplet fluid dynamics using Shmygleba's model, which is shown to be critical for accurately capturing physical phenomena. Numerical experiments are conducted, demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach.

We explore the metric dimension problem on graphs, focusing on its complexity in parameterized complexity theory. The problem involves identifying a minimum-size subset of vertices, S, in a given graph G, such that every pair of vertices in G can be uniquely identified by their distances to vertices in S. Unlike previous research, our approach does not assume the graph is given with additional information, and instead, we analyze the problem based on different structural parameters.

Our main results show that even when using the feedback vertex group as a parameter, or when combining it with graph size, the metric dimension problem is a strongly NP-hard decision problem. Furthermore, we prove the problem is W[1]-hard when parameterized by the size of a distance-based structural parameter, k, and a subset of vertices, S, that uniquely identifies all vertices in G within a given distance.

To address these parameters, we develop a lower bound parameterization for a related problem, where we aim to find a minimum-size subset of vertices, S, in the square of graph G, such that each vertex outside of S is at a distance of at least 2 from some vertex in S. Our analysis shows this problem is FPT when parameterized by the feedback vertex group and the size of a dominating set in graph G, and we provide an algorithm running in time O*(2^(g*sqrt(g)+k)+k^2).

Geometric measure theory has seen significant advancements in its interaction with functional analysis over recent decades. This paper builds on previous extensions of the Hausdorff plane to encompass complex-valued power frameworks of directed spaces. Additionally, it investigates the conditions under which oriented planes can be embedded into power frameworks of directed areas, as well as the continuous nature of area-preserving maps between these frameworks.

Earth-like atmospheres on planets near stars in the habitable zone may experience extreme climate fluctuations due to their low orbital inclinations and narrow ellipses. When one side is in constant daylight, a phenomenon known as the "substellar point" emerges, where intense solar radiation creates a hot environment. Our experiments with 3D climate models have shown that the substellar point on "habitable" and "hothouse" planets exhibits unique weather patterns, characterized by repeated cycles of cloud formation and rain. In hothouse planets, these cycles occur more frequently, and are followed by even hotter days. Our simulations suggest that the frequency and intensity of these extreme climate fluctuations depend on atmospheric water vapor, which in turn affects the planet's temperature and weather patterns.

Building on crepner's algebraic-geometric approach to crepions, a more general method is established for crepion-like extensions of self-dual Yang-Mills on complex quadrics, extending it to include elevated-spin extensions. This method is particularly relevant in the context of the twistor correspondence, which connects complex quadrics to complex projective spaces, and it specifically considers the case of $Z_4 = Q_6 \to \mathbb{CP}^3$. This paper focuses on the spin extensions of the self-dual Yang-Mills equation in complex quadric crepion spaces, which come in two distinct types. These spin extensions are found to correspond to the crepion extensions of the twistor lifts of anti-self-dual instantons in $\mathbb{R}^4$ and complex projective space $\mathbb{CP}^3$, respectively, which correspond to crepions under the Cremona transformation. To gain a deeper understanding of the spin extensions of the self-dual Yang-Mills equation, a study of the crepion elevations of anti-self-dual twistor lifts of instantons in $\mathbb{R}^4$ is carried out. A focus is placed on the properties of these spin crepion elevations, which are characterized by their behavior in terms of holomorphic functions, algebraic varieties, and meromorphic functions, which can be studied in the context of the crepion elev

Deep learning techniques have greatly improved efficiency in diagnosing multiple diseases from CT scans, but training these models on large-scale, high-quality medical image datasets is labor-intensive due to the need for professional labeling. Real-world medical image datasets are often plagued by label inaccuracies due to various factors such as human error and equipment limitations. In this research, a novel method called BARM, a Bayesian-driven framework, is proposed to enhance the classification accuracy and robustness of deep neural networks by improving the labeling quality of medical image datasets. BARM utilizes Bayesian prediction to identify and rectify label errors by leveraging the prediction distributions of pre-trained classifiers, using model uncertainty to determine labeling difficulty and guiding deep label quality improvement. Experimental evaluations on two publicly available datasets reveal significant performance improvements by BARM over five widely-used methods. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of key components within BARM.

Consider the class of functions that are composed solely of bounded one-dimensional functions from the Wiener algebra. A specific interpolation operator has been introduced in connection with the 2^k-SPONSHN grid, and it is associated with a given constant. A notable illustration has been provided, highlighting the optimality of this estimation in the context of the suggested interpolation operator and its connection to Lebesgue numbers.

A non-negative matrix's permanence ensures the results of non-negative numbers enter the stronger range. Leveraging the Featured Polynomial Related Random Walk (FPRRW) and its connection to random walk reliability, we explore its significance in network theory, particularly on directed and undirected networks where its applications extend to various critical issues, including food web stability and Google's PageRank algorithm.

Discrete time systems are often effectively modeled using inductive-recursive definitions. However, when modeling such systems with real time semantics, a time incrementing operator is necessary, which leads to a circular dependency in type definitions. In this paper, we propose an iterative solution to this problem by introducing a fixed point operator, which aligns with an eager time incrementing strategy commonly implemented in hardware. We illustrate the feasibility of this approach by applying it to a timed process definition in TCS, HOL's temporal logic.

To develop a comprehensive framework for predicting the behavior of wall-bounded turbulent flows, we first establish a correlation between specific turbulent structures and mean flow characteristics. Next, we refine the contributions of each turbulent structure to the overall Reynolds shear stress using a multi-factor weighting process, taking into account their spatial relationships and the overall energy distribution. As a result, several improved models for the near-wall region are created, showing better accuracy in the experimentally studied regimes compared to the original coherent structure-based approach. These enhanced models will lay the groundwork for further research, particularly in accounting for the outer region turbulence and the effects of varying boundary conditions.

We establish the existence of self-dual solitons within a Born-Infertile Skyrme model by utilizing variational techniques, thus enabling us to establish a minimal energy lower bound. These novel solitons allow for a lower energy limit that is lower than any classical topological soliton. Additionally, our analysis reveals that the minimal energy bound can be achieved in the asymptotic limit, a phenomenon observed when the Born-Infeld parameter tends towards infinity.

We are studying the Hofstadest model of the Weyh semimetal using a comprehensive approach. Our analysis reveals that the oscillations in the Hall conductivity behave similarly to the classic quantized Hall effect, exhibiting characteristics of the quantum interference effect, particularly in the lattice of the Dirac semimetal when under intense magnetic fields. The disruption of chiral edge modes by the magnetic field leads to the emergence of new in-volvement states, which give rise to Hall conductivity. The comprehensive model also indicates the presence of in-volvement current in the massive state and offers potential for chiral mode restoration in the high magnetic field environment.

We have developed an hybrid nano antenna design, consisting of a nano disk and two nano rods, capable of producing high-quality sources of light with a remarkable $10^6$ figure of merit. This innovative setup combines a silicon nano disk with a gold nano antenna to achieve un directional and efficient light emission with high brightness. Our experiments have confirmed that varying the gap between the nano disk and antenna has a minimal effect on the coupling gap but a significant impact on the radiation pattern. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that this hybrid antenna can be utilized as a laser cavity when paired with a gain medium, such as graphene, resulting in lasing along with significant enhancement in directional light emission. Our simulations have also shown that this setup can produce six orders of magnitude in directional enhancement gain, along with substantial reductions in the half-width of the radiation spectrum. Lastly, our research has established its potential for integrating graphene as a gain medium with perowskite slabs, yielding substantial light emission with high brightness.

According to renowned physicist Richard Feynman, an introduction to Feynman's Anomalous Shielding Theory is insufficient, highlighting the complexity of deriving the electrostatic properties of conductive fluids and granular substances from fundamental principles. This paper presents and validates a novel approach that allows for a simplified derivation of Feynman's Anomalous Shielding Theory. The proposed method can be effectively implemented using the Particle Mesh Ewald approach to solve the Poisson equation, involving three key assumptions: the presence of a vast number of conductive substance particles, uniform inter-particle spacing, and a large number of particles within the subsystem under consideration. These conditions enable a simplified derivation of Feynman's Anomalous Shielding Theory. Additionally, this approach can be used to numerically generate electrostatic potentials and probability density functions for subsystems consisting of conductive substance particles under various conditions.

Utilizing first-principles calculations, our research focuses on the properties of a silicene monolayer Mn decorated with Mn. The findings indicate that in this Mn adorned silicene structure, there is no charge transfer between Mn and silicene atoms. The presence of Mn atoms increases the lattice's vibrational density of states, resulting in a reduction of the structural stability compared to pure silicene. The electronic characteristics demonstrate that Mn adorned silicene transforms from a metal to a semiconductor, exhibiting a moderate bandgap of 0.312 eV at the Gamma point. Moreover, spin-polarized calculations reveal up and down states near the bandgap, and magnetic interactions within the Mn adorned silicene structure are explored through supercell calculations. The outcomes suggest antiferromagnetic coupling as the dominant interaction type among Mn atoms, and that Mn atoms' contribution to the band structure near the bandgap enhances the semiconductor properties, making this material suitable for spintronic applications.

A widely accepted theory suggests that the majority of the material in Sgr A East resulted from the rapid fusion of a large star that exploded nearby. The goal of this research was to create a simulation of Sgr A East using this hypothesis as a starting point. By using advanced simulation techniques, we created a model of the rapidly expanding explosion. The simulation revealed that if a star were to explode close to where the center of the galaxy now is, the force of the explosion would have sent a large amount of the gas in a different direction due to the movement and positioning of the Milky Way's bulge. The location of the center of the galaxy now fits with our simulations of the interaction between the rapidly expanding explosion and the gas in the vicinity, indicating that when a star exploded, it was close to a different point than where the center of the galaxy now is. The estimated age of the explosion, around 2.5 million years, also matches our research findings.

The work presents an empirical study on the performance of artificial oversampling techniques designed to enhance the performance of artificial neural networks in multi-category text classification tasks. A dataset of English Wikipedia articles, classified by topic using BERT and BILSTM models, is employed to evaluate the efficacy of these methods. As the dataset initially exhibits a balanced distribution of categories, synthetic samples are introduced to simulate class imbalance at progressively increasing degrees of imbalance. Experiments conducted on multi-layered BILSTM models demonstrate the performance of various artificial oversampling techniques in maintaining the performance of base models under varying levels of class imbalance. Our results indicate that random oversampling yields the best performance across all levels of class imbalance. Consequently, we assert that oversampling all categories equally surpasses other methods, such as individual category fine-tuning, for multi-category text classification tasks.

Using data from U.S. regional news websites, we analyzed the amount of COVID-19-related coverage in 2020 and compared it with other topics. U.S. regional news websites provided the most comprehensive and up-to-date information on COVID-19, even though they were not as prominent as national websites. To investigate connections between various factors, we collected and processed data on COVID-19, website traffic, news readership, and population health for all 50 U.S. states. By testing a simple hypothesis, we found no support for it in our data and proposed a theoretical framework for further research to understand the relationships among COVID-19, news coverage, public health outcomes, and media consumption patterns.

A modified version of the Rapid Multipole Algorithm preserves total angular momentum by using the equation of motion to refine and adjust the traditional velocity update method. When applied to systems exhibiting equilibrium dynamics, a modified velocity formula in the rapid multipole method accurately mirrors the results obtained from the traditional approach. However, in systems governed by non-equilibrium dynamics, a direct conversion between rapid multipole and traditional multi-pole coordinates can lead to errors in angular momentum conservation due to incomplete information about the system's evolution history. To address this issue, a corrected update formula is formulated to maintain angular momentum during rapid multipole operations.

The current evaluation of the Conveyance Factor, which measures how effectively proton polarization is transmitted from the initial to final state in the process $e\vec{p}\to e\vec{p}$, has revealed that previous values calculated using a non-relativistic model were overly large. However, these exaggerated values led to the development of spurious features, such as the non-physical dependence of the Conveyance Factor on the proton's mass, which vanished in the limit of zero mass, and incorrect relationships with spatial asymmetries. By contrast, utilizing a relativistic nucleon model has yielded significantly improved values, which effectively eliminated these artificial anomalies. Furthermore, this revised relativistic model's predictions were validated against comprehensive polarization measurements from the HAPPE experiment at Jefferson Lab for specific protons with momentum transfers $\vec{q}$ and final proton momenta $\vec{p}'$.

In order to enhance the efficiency of learning from specialized models with adjustable parameters, we introduce a method that amplifies the input data. Our goal is to improve the performance of these models, particularly when they're applied to hyper-sparse learning scenarios, where the available data is extremely limited. The method works by creating a dynamic transformation of the input data based on the parameters of the expert model in question. We test and verify the effectiveness of this approach through experiments on hypersparse learning with convolutional neural networks that have translation-invariant properties. Our results demonstrate our method significantly enhances the performance of these models in the specified hyper-sparse settings.

Using ATLAS, scientists examined double Higgs boson production in conjunction with a W or Z vector boson in proton collisions, a rare occurrence that may hold evidence of new, basic forces. From 2015 to 2018, they analyzed a vast dataset, equivalent to 140 inverse femtobarns of information. Their search focused on specific combinations of final products, including WZ, ZZ, and WZ bosons paired with Higgs boson pairs in various decay patterns, such as photons and muons. After combining multiple search channels, researchers found no signs that contradicted current scientific understanding based on the Standard Model. They established upper limits of Higgs boson decay rates, ranging from 1.7 to 3.4 times the predicted Standard Model rates, depending on the specific channel.

The key to building a spin-based memory, which utilizes the ensemble of atoms as a spin maser, has been discovered. A straightforward method has been developed to simulate the maser's behavior and solve the massive state space challenge by reducing the driving and measurement processes. By utilizing a digital quantum computer, our approach not only emulates the maser but also implements maser protocols such as state preparation, spin echo, and quantum non-demolition measurement. This method is universally applicable to simulate maser-based masqubits in any maser system.

Counting K3 varieties with a specified Picard rank over $\mathbb{C}$ and with Picard groups generated by algebraic cycles amounts to computing the real dimension of a particular type of space called a Siegel quotient space. Although this dimension isn't a direct indicator of the number of such K3 varieties, examining its magnitude relative to a maximum possible value sometimes offers insights. To illustrate our approach, we'll discuss computations involving $\mathrm{GSp}_4(\mathbb{Z})$-acting spaces and highlight some practical applications of our findings.

In a supersymmetric SUGRA model with a non-standard gravitino neutralino sector, 
we propose that a decay-product neutralino serves as a dark energy candidate. The 
model supposes that the traditional Higgs bino is extremely heavy, while the 
smallest stau selectron split occurs at a significantly lower energy scale, 
resulting in a light, nearly massless stau that decays into an electron and the 
dark energy neutralino. This neutralino then later decays into a photon pair and 
an ultra-heavy Higgsino, which in turn decays into a z pair and the SUGRA 
graviton. The model suggests that the stau should be the next-to-last particle 
to exist, with its presence potentially detectable at the LHC through a series 
of reactions, including an ultra-heavy Higgsino production and subsequent decay. 
Additionally, we explore the possibility that a neutralino decaying into 
ultra-heavy Higgsinos and photons could be the cause of the observed decay of 
distant gamma-ray bursts, resulting in a detectable spectrum of extremely low 
energy photons.

The exact computation of the genus of general graphs generally incurs a non-polynomial time complexity, whereas rapid genus estimation methods are often ineffective for certain thick graphs, thus limiting their practical utility. We propose a novel algorithm for estimating the genus of thick graphs $\Gamma$, where the estimation can be performed in polynomial time relative to the total number of vertices and edges.

In this research, we investigate an asynchronous, distributed extension of the Newton method for strictly convex optimization. Unlike traditional approaches, our distributed implementation allows each agent to execute the method independently, requiring only simple communication with nearby agents to update Newton steps and approximate solution estimates. Crucially, our approach does not require agents to trust one another. By optimizing communication timing and leveraging local curvature information, we demonstrate that our method facilitates rapid convergence at a superlinear rate. Moreover, under specific conditions, we show that the convergence rate is influenced by the network structure, specifically the number of communication rounds required to optimize network connectivity. To validate the efficacy of our method, we conduct a numerical analysis focusing on the strict convexity assumption and explore the impact of reduced communication frequency on convergence rates.

Our research examines novel techniques to detect hate speech on Twitter, including preprocessing and feature extraction using Part-of-Speech tagging, and the effectiveness of feature selection via algorithms. We investigate the relative performance of key neural network models, including Bi-LSTM, Transformer, and Autoencoder networks, in training and predicting hate-speech categories, and assess the performance of feature extraction models, including CWS and UPOS. Additionally, we evaluate the performance of feature selection algorithms, such as Genetic and Heuristic, and the impact of neural network model configurations, including reducing the Bi-LSTM network's input dimensionality, and our findings indicate that our approach yields better results than comparable studies on English and Hindi languages.

To enhance the sensitivity of real-time gas-based particle detectors for nuclear and atomic physics, it's essential to improve the understanding of recoil detection mechanisms in the existing technology, such as gas time projection chambers. This measurement campaign, called THEMIS, will assess the reaction cross sections for a range of helium isotopes when bombarded with alpha particles. Our research focuses on developing a mathematical framework to describe recoil detection, crucial for real-world gas-based detectors. This approach is based on a simple physical model incorporating the specific characteristics of helium release and ionization in different gas mixtures or blending ratios. Additionally, it's a versatile tool, applicable to other physical or nuclear physics experiments.

Driving assessments utilizing simulators have been recognized as valuable and safe alternatives in training drivers. Nonetheless, there have been concerns about their potential to foster implicit biases among instructors and students, leading to unfair evaluations. To address these concerns, the use of human-level expertise in moderating driving evaluations has been recommended. To facilitate this, a novel open-source middleware framework has been developed, integrated with a commercial driving simulation platform, to provide transparent, real-time feedback on simulator outputs. This tool enables expert modulators to effectively filter out implicit biases and make informed moderation decisions based on the simulation data.

This year's task involved creating a tool to accurately parse out of pre-defined lists and punctuation in text data. To test accuracy, we assessed metrics like table accuracy and quote accuracy based on precise matches. To improve our accuracy in this task, we needed to develop a parser capable of handling complex and ambiguous components. Two pre-trained models, ALBERT and BERT, were fine-tuned for in-text classification to increase our model's depth. The combination of these models and a custom-designed neural network resulted in the best performance seen so far, ultimately achieving a highly impressive table accuracy rate of 80.1%.

In various nonlinear field systems, stochastic dynamics along complex, high-dimensional manifolds are investigated using geometric techniques. It's discovered that the most effective pathways for particles to follow can be characterized by a generalized equation that takes into account the variations in the landscape. A comparison is made in contexts where stochastic dynamics can be described in both spatial field terms and parameter space terms. It's found that geodesic braid points provide a coherent connection between these two descriptions and offer additional benefits. Specifically, geodesic braid points not only increase robustness but also simplify understanding of topological effects. As an example, in a non-trivial gauge field environment, geodesic pathways are used to explore phenomena such as non-Abelian adiabatic effects, non-Abelian adiabatic resonance, stochastic quantum Hall effect, stochastic Chern number, stochastic Chern-Simons action, stochastic Hall conductivity, stochastic Chern-Simons equation, and stochastic Hall conductivity corrections due to finite mass effects.

This film, "Duration matters, occasionally," is an exploration of the creative process behind our film "Enchanted Forest," which was nominated for a Best Short Film at the Glasgow Film Week. In a 50-minute self-reflexive structure, the film is divided into three 16:9 segments, each with a distinct aspect ratio that breaks down into nine 7:9 screens, symbolizing the choppiness of our editing process. Our film "Duration matters occasionally" examines the concept of time in relation to editing, focusing on "enforced patience" – a state where the audience is compelled to wait for the narrative to progress. Each screen represents a different phase of our experimental editing process, from initial attempts to more refined iterations, as we grapple with the technical limitations and creative constraints. The final segment of the film is a reflection on the final editing decision-making process, which we feel has ultimately failed, but the decision to present the film in its incomplete state was a deliberate artistic choice.

Woodall previously found a constant such that all special L-values for modular forms of any weight have factorials that divide this constant raised to a power. We expand on his finding by examining the boundedness of analogous values for three different types of modular structures: those with a dual, those of Hamilton-Eberhard, and those of Katsura-Matsuno.

The behavior of electronic transport in certain types of graphene nanomaterials can be controlled and tuned, which has significant implications in various fields. Our investigation has shown that these materials can support a particular type of transport known as the spin-dependent Friedel oscillation. These oscillations arise when the electronic states of the nanomaterials are asymmetric, allowing for efficient transfer of angular momentum and charge. As a result, the conductivity of the nanomaterials becomes dependent on the spin configuration of the incoming electrons. Furthermore, our analysis has revealed that adjusting the spin of the electrons passing through the nanomaterials can significantly enhance their electronic performance. By doing so, the nanomaterials become potential candidates for various spintronic devices, such as memory and sensors.
This paper presents approximate versions of the Korovkin theorems for strongly regular operators that are either monotonic or semi-linear.

A graph is considered pancyclic if it contains cycles with every possible length from 3 to n, where n is the number of vertices. The Nordhaus-Gallai number of a graph, denoted as k, has a established link with pancyclicity; in 1978, Erdos established that an k-by-(n-k+1) complete bipartite graph contains a cycle of every possible length. Recently, Li investigated the Nordhaus-Gallai number in relation to graphs with a Hamiltonian property and determined the minimum k for which such a graph would contain a cycle of every possible length. Our paper builds on this research, connecting the Hamiltonian, Nordhaus-Gallai numbers, and pancyclic numbers in graphs of a given order.

A new approach has been developed to identify and analyze optical hadrons using time-projection-chamber-like patterns of energy and particle multiplicity in the flow data from gold-gold and isobar collisions at a specific energy level. By applying this novel technique, we discovered that the presence of optical hadrons in central collisions can be better understood in relation to the arrangement of their guiding paths' shapes in the same energy collisions, while traditional correction methods fail. Furthermore, we observed that the hadrons' movement in central Au+Au collisions differs from that in central Pb+Pb and Ru+Ru collisions. Notably, we found that these hadrons' behavior is closely related to the arrangement of the nuclear charge they collide with, which is consistent with expectations, while conventional explanations cannot fully account for this behavior.

The recent Successive Order-Hold Koopman estimator has shown considerable promise in identifying complex nonlinear systems, yet it's limited to low-dimensional systems and can struggle when data is contaminated by noise, resulting in inaccurate estimations and instability. We propose enhancing the Spectral Koopman driver by integrating the Driven Koopman Koopman estimator to tackle high-dimensional sparse data and then adapting the successively identified model using the former. We test our approach on a multi-dimensional chaotic Lorenz system and compare it to the existing Successive Order-Hold Koopman estimator in scenarios involving various noise levels. The results demonstrate that the combined technique surpasses the existing one and is capable of handling systems with considerable dimensionality.

A new efficient approach has been proposed for calculating properties of complex systems like atoms and molecules in high-intensity DC fields. This method builds upon the well-established VSCF approach, incorporating Moyal's phase space formalism. A significant advantage of this scheme is that it bypasses the need for a specialized second-order perturbation theory. Instead, it involves a preliminary calculation using the Pauli or Dirac Hamiltonian, with the computational cost being comparable to that of a Multi-Configuration Self-Consistent Field (MC-SCF) calculation. This is because the most challenging task in VSCF is obtaining a preliminary wavefunction, which can be achieved with the same level of effort as with VMCF. Following this, Moyal's formalism allows for a straightforward and accurate description of complicated scaling (CS) without external forces. This involves representing the system's wavefunction and energy in terms of the wavefunction and energy gap under no external influence. This approach has been tested and shown to be highly accurate and reliable, with results comparable to VSCF for CS without DC fields, and high precision in strong DC fields, achieving accuracy of better than 10^-4. Additionally, this scheme reveals that the effect of DC fields on low-lying bound states is relatively small, with this effect being accurately described by first-order perturbation theory, even in the case of complex atomic ions.

This paper investigates the convergence rate of the Sinkhorn algorithm in a modified scenario. In traditional approach, it divides zero entries in the cost matrix to circumvent singularities, but this method is eschewed in our specific context - where infeasible transport plans exist due to mismatched marginals. We establish a new framework in which the Sinkhorn algorithm converges to the Bregman projection onto the set of feasible transport plans, thus solving an optimal transport issue despite a lack of closed-form solution. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the algorithm's convergence rate is directly proportional to the distance between the marginal distributions. In a subsequent section, building upon recent findings, we explore how different methods can address optimal transport issues with degenerate cost matrices.

We measured the production cross-section of top-quark pairs created via hard parton collisions at the LHC. Using 252 nanobarns of data collected at a 5.02 TeV center-of-mass energy in 2017, we analyzed events featuring either one or two isolated high-energy leptons and corresponding jets, including at least two b-quark jets. By combining our findings with predictions from next-to-next-to-leading-order quantum chromodynamics theory, we found the total creation cross-section of top-quark pairs at 21.2 $\pm$ 1.0 (statistical) $\pm$ 1.0 (systematic) $\pm$ 0.4 (luminosity) teraelectronvolts, which is consistent with the standard model's expectations.

A central linkage in complex networks refers to connections that begin and end at the central node. Researchers have found that central linkages are prevalent in various real-world networks, including those representing internet protocols and food networks, and can be effectively modeled in random networks with central linkages. In networks with high central linkage concentrations, low-degree nodes often cluster around the central node and its immediate surroundings, exhibiting centralized characteristics similar to high-degree nodes. As a result, the central hub behaves as if it were a low-degree node situated at the center of a central linkage. Furthermore, when the network degree follows a power-law distribution, the central hub's connectivity grows faster than any other node's, and it begins with a connectivity of approximately N^(1/3), where N is the total number of nodes.

Our research establishes a specific condition ensuring that a Bessel-Jacobi function satisfies multiple inequalities simultaneously, while also providing sufficient conditions for the reverse implication to hold. Furthermore, precise boundaries for key parameters (including $ \alpha$, $ \beta$, $ \gamma$, and $ \delta$) are determined. The outcomes of our study have practical applications in providing unique representations for these Bessel-Jacobi functions in terms of Poisson-type integral expressions.

Few studies have explored the collective behavior of people in urban settings. However, previous non-urban studies demonstrated that non-malicious collisions between agents adhere to statistical laws similar to those observed in high-speed physics, indicating an underlying complexity in urban interactions. A notable limitation of earlier studies was their reliance on controlled environments, thus failing to account for the potential impact of pandemics on such interactions. To address this, our two-part study utilized high-speed recording devices placed within actual pedestrian crowds to examine how the COVID-19 pandemic influenced urban interactions. The results revealed significant modifications in two key characteristics: the frequency of collisions and the speed at which they occur. Furthermore, our data indicated that the distributions of these modifications followed a power-law pattern, with parameters that increased as velocity rose. Notably, our experiments showed that modifications did not change when social distancing measures were implemented, despite the agents' awareness of one another. The modifications observed during the pandemic were further exacerbated by the agents' awareness of social distancing, thus contributing to a significant increase in disparities in movements.

This research delves into novel field-separated preconditioners for multiphysics simulations of complex porous media. Building upon the successful application of field-separated techniques in petroleum engineering, this study explores their potential in geology by examining fluid flow within a heterogeneous rock formation, characterized by irregularly varying permeability levels. By comparing these preconditioners' effectiveness in such a realistic scenario, this study contributes to the development of more accurate geological models and insights into fluid dynamics in porous media.

Due to the inherent chiral nature of light's interaction with matter, many chemical and physical properties exhibit unidirectionality and asymmetry under mirror reflection. We have developed an innovative approach to creating unidirectional systems based on dielectric confinement of light using materials that have a specific chemical composition. Building upon recent breakthroughs in ultra-small, chiral materials made of silicon, our design features a microscopic optical cavity with dimensions as small as a few hundred nanometers. These structures not only support the light's chemical composition, but also act as a chemical generator, thereby achieving a level of chemical autonomy. This achievement holds great promise for the development of future integrated photonic systems that replicate natural chemical and physical processes.

We derive the 1-loop boundary 1-point function for bosonic string scattering and establish its connection to JT gravity behavior near AdS_2, which is determined by the string's Regge slope and the boundary's cosmological constant. As such, JT gravity behavior encodes some 1-loop string theory information. It is also found that a specific redefinition of the boundary cosmological constant allows the 1-loop boundary 2-point function to be expressed within the framework of random unitary matrices.

Einstein's field equations with a cosmological constant $\Lambda$ are investigated, specifically within the context of warping the $xt$-plane using the Miller-Tavakol warp metric's topology. Two distinct scenarios are explored: the presence of a massless fluid and a massive fluid. Our analysis reveals that the massless fluid scenario has a singular point at $\Lambda=0$, whereas the massive fluid scenario allows for non-zero values of $\Lambda$, $k$, and $m$. Consequently, mass is generally linked to fluctuations in $\Lambda$ and the fluid density, particularly its pressure.

New York City's Guiding Arts & Design in EnvironmentS initiative, a spatial information framework, is subject to the limit of coordinate precision set by the EPSG:4326 standard. This results in a measurable error, approximately 14 cm, in represented locations at the maximum. To mitigate this error, NYC has taken steps to localize its reference data by converting spatial information to a local coordinate system. However, this transition poses the challenge of synchronizing multiple datasets with spatial resolutions that range widely. To address this, GUIDES has established detailed technical specifications for key resolution levels. These standards define specific pixel and line counts for various scales, with a focus on levels 7 through 10. Each resolution level is assigned a specific number of pixels and lines, with associated ground distances. For instance, level 8 features 256 pixels and lines with a ground distance of about 12.5 m. GUIDES has further specified that for each resolution level, the Geospatial Citywide Model (GCM) layer, the Citywide Asset Registry (CAR) feature collection, and the 3D model collection should adhere to these specific resolutions to ensure consistency.

In the strong-coupling regime of a two-dimensional Lattice of Ions, our experiments reveal how the decay of spin is influenced by transverse lattice motions. Our measurements confirm that equidistributed phonon mode temperatures lead to rapid spin-spin decoherence and ion heating, as opposed to scenarios where only transverse modes are heated, under both conditions where the spin is parallel and anti-parallel to the motion, resulting in significantly longer coherence times in the latter. These findings align well with calculations based on perturbation theory. Moreover, our experiments also show that the rate at which transverse modes are heated is directly related to spin-spin decoherence rates. By varying key parameters, we have verified an observed linear relationship between the two and determined the maximum error margin of approximately 10%. Consequently, our experiments also validate the adiabatic approximation even at high ratios of coupling and phonon frequencies.

A method has been introduced to quantify the impact of chemistry and electromagnetic factors in TERS experiments. This was accomplished by comparing theoretical and experimental spectra across various scenarios. These factors were analyzed in systems consisting of a single- or double-metal atom on a nanoparticle that produces a strong electromagnetic field in the aperture of a nanotip. Chemically, different metal-carbon bonds were studied between the free metal atom and a substrate. In all these cases, the CNT's substrate resonance remained constant. It was found that: (a) electromagnetic factors dominate experiments where only one metal atom is present; and (b) experiments involving a double-metal atom are influenced by the substrate resonance's electromagnetic enhancement, as well as by chemical modifications of both the free and substrate metal. Furthermore, it was confirmed that the observed spectral shifts are a mix of electromagnetic and chemical influences.

We investigated the Spectral Energy Distribution of a 31 selected galaxy, including our own Milky Way. The galaxies were chosen randomly from a sample of spiral galaxies located at a distance of up to 20 Mpc within the Northern sky. The detection of anomalous microwave emission in extragalactic systems is crucial for developing theoretical models explaining its physical basis. Utilizing the Sardinia Radio Dish, our research yielded significant results, revealing that the SDE exhibits brighter millimeter emission than previously estimated. Additionally, we discovered that the SDE has an unusually steep spectral index, characterized by $\alpha \sim 2.2$. Notably, we found that SdM1 exhibits emission across all frequencies, although the SNE does not demonstrate similar microwave emission. We observed SDE2 exhibit emission across all frequencies, alongside SDE3, which displays emission in the K-band. Our analysis of the K-band data enabled us to derive constraints on the SDE, which is the strongest yet obtained, along with SDE1, which demonstrates an upper limit of $S_{86.52\ GHz} < 22.4$ mJy. We found the 86.52 GHz constraints on SNe to be the most stringent, which could be instrumental in refining constraints on the ionization fraction of the IGM.

Thermoelectric materials with the ability to produce a significant change in entropy in response to electric fields are called electrocaloric materials. Ammonium sulfate exhibits electrocaloric, ferroelectric and piezoelectric properties. At 120 K, ammonium sulfate displays a significant entropy alteration of -0.13 JK^-1kg^-1 in the electric field in the range of 0.1 to 2.0 MK, making it a promising material for significant entropy enhancement. Investigations have revealed that the significant entropy alteration in ammonium sulfate is caused by the orientation of dipoles, and the phase transition is ferroelectric in nature, as confirmed by infrared spectroscopy and dielectric measurements. The entropy change is attributed to the substantial increase in entropy resulting from the phase transition in ammonium sulfate.

In reinforcement learning (RL), creatures and animals strive to maximize their rewards by deciding between multiple options through repeated trials, constantly adjusting their choices based on the actual versus expected rewards they receive from selected actions. Although the standard RL algorithms from control theory are considered optimal under specific simplifying conditions, they aren't always seen in real-world learning behaviors. To investigate the prevalence of standard RL algorithms in nature, we conducted an experiment involving 28 human participants who learned to choose between multiple options in an environment similar to that studied by a computer simulation of two RL models. Notably, the human learning behavior significantly aligned with the non-optimal model featuring time-limited reward updates. However, the optimal model showed a stronger correlation with brain activity in the reward prediction discrepancy region. These findings indicate that, while humans predominantly struggle to achieve optimal results, neural mechanisms underlying learning may still align closely with optimal strategies.

A proposed approach leveraging the $E_8$ root system in its complex form may uncover the deep interconnections between quantum entanglement and contextuality. By analyzing the directed graph derived from this structure, we discover an extensive collection of Hamiltonian measurements in pairs, exhibiting a rich pattern of contextual behavior. Notably, measurements within each pair become compatible solely upon the presence of a specific intermediate measurement. Ultimately, we establish that the directed graph's vertex set provides an exceedingly vast reservoir of multi-partite quantum states across different systems.

This study investigates the multi-dimensional close-neighbor problem in a geometric context where we're dealing with the $\varepsilon$-approximation of the minimum distance metric along the $L_\infty$ scale. To address this issue efficiently, researchers have previously proposed an algorithm with nonlinear query time complexity of $N^\varepsilon$ and linear build complexity. This paper specifically addresses the subset of the close-neighbor problem known as the approximate close-neighbor issue, differing in that the aim is to locate the point that's optimally close, rather than all points within an $\varepsilon$ margin. A key aspect involves developing data structures where the measured distance is at least $(1-\delta)$ times the minimum distance for any queried point, given an arbitrarily small $\delta > 0$. We introduce a reduction of this problem to the offline velocity range searching problem, subsequently establishing that it involves finding the shortest path in a graph with polynomial complexity in the number of vertices, both in terms of query and preprocessing costs. We then employ an existing solution of the velocity range searching problem, adapting it to accommodate an additional $\delta$ factor. To complement its efficiency, a lower bound of $\Omega(n^{1/2-\chi})$ query time is proved for its solution, involving arbitrarily small $\chi > 0$, assuming the standard conjecture of the Orthogonal Vectors Problem.

In the context of adaptive clinical trials, accurate respondent selection is crucial for both safety and trial success, as it is heavily influenced by the accuracy of psychometric assessments. Unfortunately, many high-precision tests often result in inconsistent scoring among different raters. By treating the assessment errors as random noise, we can utilize a Bayesian model in an iterative process to enhance the reliability of these ratings and reduce rating discrepancies. Through simulated trials, we found that our method effectively decreases the level of inconsistency among different ratings and improves both real-world trial performance and original statistical power.

To effectively manage complex and dynamic environments, robots require the ability to adapt autonomously and collaborate closely. By employing autonomy in pairs, robots can not only regulate and coordinate their own actions but also safely and reliably interact with one another and their surroundings. We propose a framework based on autonomous cooperation that enables and manages collaborative interactions between robots and their environment. We will demonstrate the feasibility of this approach in two scenarios - a shared-robotics scenario and an autonomous vehicle scenario - which involve multiple robots interacting with their environment and one another. These scenarios aim to address challenges related to inter-robot interaction and shared-robotics, respectively. Ultimately, we aim to show how and when collective autonomy can lead to meaningful inter-robot interactions.

Existing map representations, such as 2D images, text descriptions, and related data, struggle to effectively support navigation in unfamiliar environments. Two main issues arise from current representations, which are either ambiguous in conveying spatial relationships (like 2D images and text descriptions) or highly inefficient in processing due to requiring specific knowledge and setups (like 3D models and knowledge graphs). To address these challenges, we propose HiTMap, an innovative method to represent unfamiliar environments as a hierarchical two-dimensional directed graph, which clearly conveys spatial relationships and supports navigation based on basic knowledge. By introducing explicit self-supervised learning, HiTMap enables text-based visual map understanding without the need for external labeled datasets. To further enhance its functionality, we also introduce HiNavi, a novel navigational assistant that leverages HiTMap and achieves state-of-the-art performance in both navigation and visual language navigation.

In this research, we propose innovative methodologies to generate inter-group supplementary code sets and multidimensional binary array code sets, building upon existing frameworks, such as the BS code set. Our developed sets exhibit unique properties, specifically inter-group orthogonality and high packing efficiency. Additionally, we introduce a general approach for two-dimensional zero-correlation zone supplementary array code set generation based on multi-variable Boolean functions, enabling the efficient packing of multiple code sets with varying correlation zones. The effectiveness of our proposed methods is demonstrated through thorough theoretical analysis and comparative evaluations with established frameworks.

Computational tomography reconstructs internal structures from multiple external measurements, but using radiations of varying frequencies can lead to inaccuracies, a phenomenon known as chromatic aberration, causing image blur. By leveraging and extending the success of full tensor reconstruction, we can adapt these techniques to address polyenergetic CT image degradation, where color channels depend on energy levels. Our approach involves a multi-step process: first, we model the various polyenergetic CT sources available; second, we propose a non-negative matrix decomposition-based reconstruction technique where the decoding matrix corresponds to the common chromatic aberration transformation matrix; third, we incorporate a probabilistic model where the images and scaling matrix serve as representations and precisions of the chromatic aberration, allowing us to address image denoising through root decomposition. Our simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, showcasing its ability to handle multiple sources and reduce sensor noise in the computed tomography domain.

A two-band model incorporating electron outflow is employed to investigate two-dimensional and three-dimensional systems containing metallic and semiconducting regions. In particular, a rigorous analysis of one-dimensional electron outflow boundaries in a two-band nonlocal model is performed, and existence and positivity proofs for the dielectric function in the case of a single-layered gap plasmon are obtained. Furthermore, the research includes numerical studies of higher-order gap plasmons in multi-layered structures with increasingly smaller intervals, and we show that the potential energy density remains strictly positive even in this case. These findings confirm and expand upon earlier results in which the potential energy density was proven to be positive for one-dimensional gap plasmons in a two-dimensional and three-dimensional electron gas. In addition, the two-band model considers the general case of dielectric and metallic configurations and we demonstrate that the potential energy density is positive under certain conditions.

In contextual named entity recognition (CNE), the challenge of a term's appearance in one position not reflecting its relevance in another is referred to as the "term location bias." This issue causes models to struggle with accurate CNE predictions. To address this, researchers have discovered that incorporating a word's importance across various terms, represented by the term importance feedback (TIB) effect, can aid in recovering contextual named entities. Building on this insight, a model combining the attention mechanisms at the pixel and term levels (PAB and TAB) is proposed to leverage the term importance feedback effect for contextual named entity recognition. Experimental results on the BioBERT-NER and xLM-Twitter18 datasets reveal that the proposed PAB and TAB models significantly outperform existing top-performing models in CE and CNE tasks.

To enhance interaction with linear data, we extend its complexity by introducing a sequential dimension. This enables us to detect patterns not easily visible in its 2D representation. However, sequentially displayed data can be cumbersome to navigate. To address this challenge, we introduce interactive features that streamline exploration of this additional dimension. Our approach is demonstrated through an application in identifying anomalies during World War II battles, which can also benefit other fields.

Using electronic health records to predict a patient's future similar patients can aid clinicians in making more informed decisions and improve patient care quality and outcomes. Traditional methods that simply match textual medical descriptions overlook essential contextual information about the causes and effects of diseases, as well as diverse patient characteristics. This paper proposes a novel approach that simultaneously considers contextual and heterogeneous patient features to identify patients with similar clinical outcomes. Our dynamic approach identifies causal factors and incorporates them into patient comparison, while an adversarial module removes context-specific characteristics to enable context-agnostic matching. Experiments on two digital health datasets show that our approach outperforms baseline methods in identifying patients with similar clinical outcomes.

This study explores the impact of solvent polarization on the electric double layer (EDL) of soft interfaces using a coarse-grained molecular dynamics approach. An analytical model combining a Poisson-Boltzmann equation and a Debye-H\"uckel equation describes the electrostatic and hydrodynamic interactions between solvent dipoles, solvent ions, and surface macromolecules. By comparing simulation and analytical results for solvents with diverse dielectric constants and ion valences, this study demonstrates that solvent polarization significantly affects model systems within the 1 M concentration range, with potential implications for real-world systems.

This study investigates and builds on common practices for extracting software specifications from informal sources such as emails, forum posts, and social media comments. We examine the underlying challenges and examine data-driven approaches to tackle these issues, including leveraging knowledge graphs to infer software specifications from unscheduled texts. Our analysis reveals that a small subset of software entities and features accounts for the majority of extraction tasks, simplifying the overall problem.

A growing number of wireless devices in both urban and rural settings has led to the creation of dense networks, which in turn are prone to energy loss and inefficiency. To address this challenge, the concept of collaborative networking allows relays to take turns sleeping and waking up, thereby enhancing both energy efficiency and data transmission rates. This paper focuses on optimizing the network's energy efficiency by combining the selection of relays, their active durations, and power distribution in a unified framework, where the objective is to minimize the total power consumption per successful data delivery while maintaining or improving the overall transmission rate. The optimization problem is reformulated, and a novel algorithm called Energy Efficient Network Encoding with Joint Relay selection and Power distribution (EE-NEC-JRSP) is developed, which uses joint relay selection and power distribution to achieve superior energy efficiency compared to existing solutions. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm, which, under high noise conditions, saves approximately 1.7 times more power than energy-optimal power allocation, and comparable to cooperative encoding-based relaying, while achieving 96.2% power savings compared to traditional network encoding.

This study applies the Initial Principles Theory of Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (IPOS) states to various magnetic adsorbates placed on superconducting surfaces, specifically examining the properties of Sc and Mn adsorbates on a superconducting Nb surface over several years of research, specifically initial studies in 2013-2014 and more recent studies in 2021-2022. The current work specifically examines the spectral properties of Sc and Mn adsorbates using data from two experiments, and compares these properties with simulations. The simulations use superconducting parameters of Nb and local exchange interaction parameters for Sc and Mn. The spectral properties of Sc and Mn are shown to be consistent with experimental data. The study also examined the spectral properties of Sc and Mn adsorbates in specific configurations on the Nb surface, specifically the (110) surface. The spectral properties of Sc and Mn adsorbates were simulated in various configurations and the results were consistent with experimental data. The spectral properties of Sc and Mn adsorbates were found to be consistent with the measurements and the exchange parameters used.

This research addresses the issue of bias in deep learning-based 3D object detection systems, which can result in unequal performance across different categories due to uneven data distribution. Our approach involves the implementation of a 6-degree-of-freedom (6DoF) scan alignment method based on a neural network filter to eliminate the influence of biased parameters. By analyzing the connection between scan matching accuracy and prejudice, we established the necessary conditions for bias-reduced scan alignment and developed an approach grounded in density ratio estimation. Our method automatically learns the scan alignment transformation through a neural network and evaluates its effectiveness on synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating substantial enhancement in pre-training and preparation procedures for 3D detection systems.

We propose an algorithm for identifying edges in satellite images without relying on deep networks. The goal is to create a mask indicating where edges exist within satellite images. The algorithm we developed incorporates both deep networks and more efficient, streamlined techniques. The experiment involved a diverse set of satellite images collected from various sources. The results demonstrate that our algorithm achieves equivalent edge recognition accuracy to current state-of-the-art methods utilizing deep networks, while also demonstrating greater efficiency due to the incorporation of simpler techniques.

In ultra-intense X-ray free electron laser beams, the immediate surroundings of high-atomic-number atoms can become densely populated with electrons, leading to notable X-ray absorption fluctuations. Consequently, conventional techniques for studying materials, such as X-ray absorption near edge structure, become ineffective. To overcome this challenge, researchers have developed the non-linear XANES approach, a technique that accounts for electron screening and multiple photoionization in the process. To gain insight into the high-order effects of multiple photoionization in non-linear XANES spectra, researchers employed the classical screening model to calculate and analyze the rate of photoion electrons and photoelectrons. Notably, findings revealed that the photoionization rate escalates exponentially with screen charge density for outer p-shell ionization in non-linear environments, surpassing the linear regime by over two orders of magnitude. In contrast, multiple photoionization rates exhibit significant growth for inner s, p, and d shells, particularly for p and d shells, where the order of magnitude can increase by up to six. Moreover, studies indicate that the order of photoionization rates for s, p, and d shells follows the pattern s > p > d. These results highlight the potential for examining non-linear screening effects and order photoionization processes in the future. Moreover, notable trends in the order photoionization rates of valence shells and inner p, d, and f shells can be observed, paving the way for further research into the screening effects of these

This paper presents the modulation classification problem's highly reliable solution, 
which is not vulnerable to hostile attacks that commonly affect machine learning models in this area. 
A Deep Neural Network (DNN) based modulation classifier has previously been proposed in the literature, 
which can effectively classify modulations but fails to withstand hostile attacks due to its limited capability. 
In this research, a Guided Back-Propagation (GBP) attack is launched to evaluate the Deep Neural Network's (DNN) 
performance under adverse conditions. 
Subsequently, a Style Transfer (ST) attack is conducted to further examine the DNN's resilience, 
which involves moving images from different modulations while retaining the original data features. 
As a result, the DNN's performance deteriorates significantly under hostile attacks, 
which is an unexpected outcome. 
In response to this, a Contrastive Conditional Generative Adversarial Network (C-CGAN) is introduced, 
which can effectively classify modulations and avoid being affected by the GBP or ST attacks, 
demonstrating its outstanding performance under adverse conditions compared to the CGAN, 
the Radial Basis Function Neural Network (RBFNN), and the DNN models.

To develop accurate diagnostic models, large datasets are necessary, particularly in the field of neuroimaging where public datasets are scarce and small. Consequently, researchers often augment available data by combining it with data from various sources, predicting that such ensemble learning would perform better. However, our research indicates the opposite can be true as the number of domains and differences in data increase, especially concerning the classification of Multiple Sclerosis in brain MRI scans. We found educational models, though not leveraging all the data, outperformed ensemble strategies that involved multiple domains. Furthermore, we demonstrated the ability of educational models to successfully handle domain-free data from unknown sources, outperforming ensemble models on unknown domains.

A non-equilibrium, steady state is referred to as a manic state. In this state, a system confined by soft constraints undergoes continuous deformation due to external forces applied at its boundaries. We examine a manic state characterized by a long relaxation time and manage to describe the system's properties solely through its entropic constraints. This state is akin to a standard equilibrium state obtained by slowly squeezing an ideal gas under equilibrium conditions. In contrast, a manic entropy arises due to its specific geometry. We specifically analyze a system where particles move freely within a toroidal shape, formed by combining two topological directions - one with low viscosities allowing for equilibrium processes and one with high viscosities preventing equilibrium. In this scenario, a manic entropy has been topologically unified. As a result, the manic state becomes a generalized equilibrium state that can be described using Manevich's generalized thermodynamics. This process represents a novel approach to understanding soft confinement dynamics.

In complex systems research, modeling dynamic behaviors incorporates uncertainty through error margins. However, traditional approaches to accounting for model error rely on robust control theory, which doesn't consider the specific characteristics of dynamic systems, only its general properties. This paper introduces a new framework for model error in dynamic systems, incorporating information about both the system's structure and its uncertainty. We develop a differential geometry-based structure-informed model error manifold, where dynamic system structure and uncertainty contribute to a unified representation of error. This framework is demonstrated in a data-driven machine intelligence example, where a neural network learns the dynamics of a known dynamic system, along with its error structure. This leads to the creation of an informed model error manifold, which has significant benefits in dynamic systems analysis and control applications.

A black hole-driven expansion of a core is expected in star-forming regions.
This prediction has so far been validated for star-forming areas with existing stars.
We have now found a different outcome in region DR-W44, a dense area of star formation.
This region, which spans about 15.5 parsecs, is the site of enormous star formation activity and produces about 10 times the solar mass of new stars each year.
Using a combination of sub-millimeter and sub-millimeter/millimeter observations, we found that the density of this region extends to the edges of its emission.
By combining velocity and dust density data, we found evidence of expansion throughout the region.
The speed and pattern of this expansion differ at the center and edges of the region.
This is consistent with the region being expanded by a supermassive star or a black hole.
This is the first time such expansion has been found in a region where new stars are being born.
This is also the most massive region ever observed to be expanded.
This discovery has important implications for understanding the relationship between massive star formation and the expansion of their surroundings.

Recent findings from Event Horizon Telescope challenge general relativity predictions, suggesting that supermassive black holes may be unusually transparent in millimeter wavelengths, or that accretion flows are denser than anticipated. To address this, researchers are exploring the possibility that primordial black holes within a surrounding dense medium act as shading objects for the accreting material, a concept referred to as shadow matter. Our study aims to numerically verify shadow matter through PopSyCLE simulations, which simulate primordial black hole formation, evolution, and interaction with stellar radiation fields.

By analyzing a system of rigid wedge-shaped spheres, researchers discovered variations in splay angles at the interface of solid substrates and liquid crystals, leading to distinct stages of variation. This phenomenon leads to the prediction of unique planar alignment structures in certain geometric configurations of rigid spheres, contrary to established theories of liquid crystal deformation profiles. These novel configurations may have significant implications for the design of liquid crystal displays and elastic membranes.

Our goal is to adjust neural network parameters that process a specific
input, without modifying the network's core structure. We propose a novel
adaptation method called Token Adaptation (ToAd), which uniquely fine-tunes
only one token within each network block when processing a specific input. ToAd
demonstrates exceptional efficiency, surpassing traditional methods in
learning other tasks while requiring significantly fewer core network parameters.
ToAd achieves this by forcing the shared token to capture a broader range of
information and utilizing a compact, fast-swin transformer for fast adaptation.
ToAd only modifies Token Attention (TokenA), a lightweight and fast module, to
guarantee the learned adaptations are generalizable across different tasks.
ToAd's training is fully end-to-end, and we show that ToAd can reutilize
previously trained and frozen ToAd modules to adapt to new tasks. ToAd's
capability to reuse modules has not been demonstrated before, offering fast
inference and enhanced generalization. Comprehensive evaluations on a range of
visual perception tasks confirm ToAd's adaptability and state-of-the-art
performance compared to other adaptation methods.

This paper investigates the integration of a user's subjective preferences into data-driven machine learning through the lens of intrinsic and extrinsic preference ordering.  Intrinsic preference considers an item's value in isolation whereas extrinsic preference includes the item's value influenced by accompanying items within a set.  In most applications, users express their preferences in pairs rather than complete sets, making the modeling of full set preferences a crucial next step.
