The research compares non-contextual and contextual preference ordering models to accomplish this, with the former offering a straightforward, set-level approach and the contextual model requiring additional context information.  A common similarity-based method is used to expand the user's partial preferences to include more granular, contextual preferences within subsets, and then match similar contextual preferences to estimate the full set preference.  In contrast, the non-contextual approach directly learns a full set ranking and applies it to estimate the user's preferred set, without considering context.  In experiments, the proposed non-contextual approach outperforms the contextual approach by improving overall ranking accuracy and user satisfaction by 10-15%, while requiring less computational resources and model complexity.

A linear viscoelastic response function database is analyzed for randomly selected linear polymers near the glass transition temperature to uncover connections between dynamic and thermodynamic properties. When divided by the glassy specific heat, the plot of $\gamma$ versus the relaxation time $\tau_\alpha$ follows a logarithmic relationship. Furthermore, when the $\Delta C_p$ parameter is replaced with $\gamma$, a similar correlation emerges. We also validate the analysis by comparing it to the dielectric relaxation time and the distribution of relaxation times. We also test this relationship against a different temperature dataset for the same polymers. Utilizing the tool \texttt{polymer-properties}, we make the database accessible for general use. We propose that $\gamma$ is a physical parameter that plays a role in the glass transition.

In numerous ML-based systems, parameters that have been removed or over-written as the system progresses tend to lose their initial importance. Specifically, in the context of transformer-transformer training sequences, early stages tend to be overwritten by later stages. We coined the term 'Developmental Rejection Processing' to describe this phenomenon within multi-stage transformer models. Using transformer transformers for this purpose allows us to visualize the evolution of a system's capabilities across its development and accurately pinpoint crucial growth periods, particularly in systems trained with external supervision. This enables us to gain a deeper understanding of the model and its growth process.

We introduce a new creative strategy for machine interpretation that utilizes
an anticipatory approach. By predicting the response to an inquiry, we nurture
an agent's understanding to generate a response that presents a straightforward
prediction. Our implementation, built on top of a neural knowledge interpreter,
showcases an improved approach compared to a baseline with a experiment showing
the proposed approach results in a higher success rate. Additionally, we
investigate additional techniques for measuring and predicting the response in
relation to the updated knowledge, each with their own advantages and
disadvantages.

Building on previous work, a collection of graph-based formulas for the Kontsevich value, where vertices are limited to a maximum degree of P, was established to be a subset of the overall possible graph configurations. Building upon this framework, further computations revealed that the total contour curvature graphs, where vertices are constrained to be triangular, can be determined independently using only the most basic graph structure. Specifically, when considering graphs where vertices are at most decagons, it was discovered that the contour curvature graphs share a direct and proportional relationship with a previously identified set of hexagon-based graphs. This hexagon-based structure, known as the EKR graph, serves as a foundation upon which the calculation of the P=8 Kontsevich value of a quadrilateral graph was developed, with the resulting formula being the first in a series that follows a pattern similar to Pascal's triangle. Furthermore, an existing formula was proven for the purpose of calculating the P=2P-2 Kontsevich value of a 2P-gon, specifically highlighting the connection with the curvature graph of a 4P-gon.

Our research reveals that for a specific class of large-N CFTs, even the smallest deformation results in a new IR fixed point. For a broad range of deformations, we determine the location of this fixed point in the space of couplings. In contrast, for certain types of deformations such as those enhancing symmetry, a new fixed point emerges, characterized by negative central charges in 2D. Thermal and entanglement entropy analyses confirm the existence of the new fixed point, while thermal large-N expansion indicates that the system transitions to strong coupling at any non-zero temperature.

Wang, Jiang, and Wang (2020) claimed to derive a universal framework for valuing Asian options in various Markov models, but this claim invalidates many publications and even existing valuations of such options in well-known markets processes. Upon analyzing their work more closely, we find that it contains fundamental errors stemming from incorrect Theorem 1 and incorrect formula (18), which undermines the validity of their research.

Researchers suggest an alternative explanation for observed gamma-ray emissions from clusters of galaxies, proposing a broader distribution across super-structures like the Virgo Supercluster. The long-standing debate over the origin of these emissions, radio galaxies versus the cosmic ray interactions within the cluster gas, might be resolved by considering a more extensive distribution of radio galaxies. A gamma-ray distribution associated with radio galaxies would naturally follow their known spatial distribution and exhibit an elongated pattern. By relating gamma-ray brightness to the radio flux density of a galaxy group or cluster, we explore possible explanations for existing gamma-ray observations. The predicted distribution of group-and-cluster emissions would create the appearance of "gamma-ray fading flows" in the sky, potentially mimicking a large-scale flow caused by cosmic expansion.

Non-trivial inflaton scalar fluctuations, originating from the interaction of a coupled pseudoscalar field, can produce long-wavelength fluctuations that resonate and respond to short-wavelength modes. When the slow-roll of the inflatinon is suspended, these resonant scalar fluctuations are generated, which in turn may be detected through cosmological collider signals and modifications to the primordial power spectrum. Although non-standard fluctuations are not expected to significantly impact traditional cosmological collider signals during slow-roll inflation, these fluctuations can produce unique oscillatory features. These oscillations, unlike those resulting from massive long-lived particles, may offer additional insights into inflation. In order to identify these oscillations in future cosmic microwave background observations, we investigate the characteristics of these features. Our analysis shows that the power spectrum is most visibly impacted by the slow-roll parameter and order of the perturbation. Notably, this research presents a new approach for examining traditional oscillatory features.

We introduce a novel approach, the Visual-Semantic Filter Focus (V-SFF), designed to enhance explanations of Deep Convolutional Neural Networks, particularly within the context of ImageNet, for both classification and convolutional layers. Unlike existing methods, V-SFF integrates two visual perspectives for network analysis: global visual features captured by heatmaps and localized visual semantics derived from superpixels, for a more comprehensive and insightful interpretation. By employing the proposed approach, we achieve robust results on various evaluation criteria, surpassing state-of-the-art methods with more refined and insightful visualizations and more accurate and granular textual descriptions. Our comprehensive evaluation and detailed analysis of the proposed approach are available on the website http://convexoptimization.com/Ali/VCube/.

A novel phonon-assisted mechanism is explored which has the potential to induce an attractive force between electrons in one-dimensional systems. This particular mechanism surpasses the conventional short-range phonon-mediated interaction and reveals its own long-range characteristics. Specifically, a system of electrons coupled to optical phonons exhibits an associated interaction function. When electron momentum is close to the phonon momentum magnitude, the association function exhibits an interesting property where its magnitude surpasses that of a conventional, short-range electron-phonon interaction. Furthermore, a one-dimensional model of Bi$_2$SeO$_6$ was utilized to demonstrate that this phenomenon can materialize in real-world systems. Lastly, an examination of electron pairing resulting from this interaction was conducted, and it was discovered that at sufficiently strong electron-phonon coupling magnitudes and weak electron momentum conditions, competing mechanisms produce a net result akin to that of short-range electron-phonon interactions.

The examination of design or process improvements that involve multiple interrelated variables demands a complex modeling approach capable of handling vast personal-level data sets. We conducted an analysis of the enhancements in a large mental health organization, employing a combination of data and modeling techniques to learn a causal representation of the organization's structure from a single dataset of client interactions and their outcomes. By building a graphical model that captures the flow of information and its impact on the organization's results, our method automatically learns the relevant features of the process and their effects on the organization's performance. We demonstrate that this approach allows us to simulate various design scenarios, estimate their potential benefits, and provide recommendations for the organization's management. We found that our method generates highly accurate representations of the organization's structure compared to the organization's actual structure, and surpasses traditional techniques in identifying critical factors and improving organization's performance. Notably, our method achieves substantial gains in diagnostic accuracy by identifying key factors and optimizing organization's performance. We achieve these gains without relying on any domain-specific knowledge or manual specification of the organization's structure.

The metastable grid of skyrmions is a crucial structure in the context of particle physics and data storage technology. By utilizing neutron scattering and numerical simulations, we have observed the formation of lattice vortexes surrounding the skyrmions in a specific Mn-based alloy. This alloy serves as an ideal system for studying the transformation of these metastable structures. As a result, we have witnessed a phase transition from a metastable lattice of vortices and skyrmions at low temperatures to a liquid state of only vortices at higher temperatures, which is accompanied by a topological phase transition from a finite number of vortices at low temperatures to an infinite number of vortices at higher temperatures.

Social network analysis has traditionally relied on egocentric frameworks, yet recent advancements have shifted towards more interconnected models incorporating egocentric data and information from network contexts. The growing interest in high-dimensional network modeling has led to the development of innovative techniques for representing interdependent data in social networks. This work provides an in-depth examination of cutting-edge methodologies applied to the estimation of time-varying influence models for a single individual, with a particular emphasis on timeliness, simplicity, and the ability to handle interconnected dimensions. We also introduce future research inquiries aimed at addressing estimation challenges for aggregate levels, such as for entire networks or subgroups.

In recent years, the static point method has garnered increased attention due to its potential to mitigate the imbalance between data and label costs. However, its widespread adoption remains limited, partly due to the unresolved problem of unknown data class distributions in the unverified class pool. Consequently, the sampling process in this context often fails, giving rise to substantial waste in both data and label collection. To overcome these shortcomings, a novel dynamic point method has been introduced. By breaking free from the constraints of the static framework, the dynamic approach enables a more efficient sampling process, thus reducing resource waste. Furthermore, the dynamic approach can seamlessly integrate with the static method to create a unified iterative framework, which we extensively tested and demonstrated on both single-source and multi-source learning scenarios, ultimately yielding superior performance outcomes compared to the static approach and its competing counterparts.

Augmented reality has the potential to revolutionise shopping, but it is limited by the lack of reliable and secure methods for conveying information.  In order to overcome this, we have developed a highly secure method for creating AR applications, employing the latest developments in neural networks and probabilistic machine learning techniques.  This approach has significant applications in digital rights management and censorship resistance within AR.  Our novel technique for protecting AR applications is based on the concept of Bayesian neural networks, which enables us to create a password-protected system that can be removed using the correct credentials, allowing the hidden content to be retrieved and displayed when the correct password is entered.  This technique has the additional benefit of being virtually impossible to clone, as only the password holder has the ability to retrieve the concealed information.  In order to overcome the limitations of previous techniques, which often suffer from reduced visibility when retrieving the hidden content, we have developed a highly efficient method for encoding and decoding binary data, which significantly improves the overall performance and readability of the concealed content when viewed through AR.  Our technique also enables seamless integration with the AR platform, allowing users to retrieve the hidden content without interruption.  In addition to our novel encoding method, we have developed a more efficient channel for transmitting concealed content, which significantly reduces memory usage and increases the reliability of the hidden content when retrieving the hidden information.  This technique enables users to retrieve the hidden content without experiencing visual glitches or distortions.  Overall, our technique offers a highly secure

Recent advancements in mean-field dynamo theory have led to significant breakthroughs in modeling various dynamos within rotating spheres, particularly those with dynamos located away from the center. To further refine mean-field frameworks and capture the complexity of magnetic dynamos, it is essential to account for all relevant turbulent effects, such as alpha-effect, turbulent Reynolds stress and omega-effect. This study aims to develop a comprehensive mean-field framework capable of representing convective spherical dynamos, by considering a broader range of turbulent influences. We achieve this goal, by developing mean-field expressions for effects like the alpha-coefficient and turbulent Reynolds stress coefficients, taking into account arbitrary mean-field orientations and anisotropic mean-field alignment. We then utilize these expressions to create a comprehensive mean-field framework, capable of capturing dynamos with global dipolar, quadrupolar, and mixed parities. Additionally, this framework can account for phenomena such as tilt and dynamo-induced flows. We validate our approach by comparing the results from our mean-field theory with direct numerical simulations, revealing that it can accurately predict the global magnetic field and its associated mean flow for various boundary conditions. Overall, our work demonstrates that the comprehensive mean-field framework we developed is a powerful tool, particularly when accounting for higher-order parity and non-axisymmetric effects.

The center of NGC4945 is home to an extremely active galactic nucleus, where a powerful and massive galactic wind is thought to originate. Researchers used ALMA to observe a massive eruption of molecular gas in this galaxy, a colossal cloud with a mass of 1000 solar masses, moving at 700 kilometers per second. The eruption occurred in the heart of the galaxy and exhibited signs of being pushed outward rapidly, with density variations and complex patterns along its path. The dynamics of the eruption suggest it was propelled by energy rather than gas pressure, and its unique features offer valuable insights into the process by which galactic winds operate.

A novel numerical approach is developed for solving complex quasilinear diffusion equations, originally used to model the behavior of high-energy particles in plasas. This approach is rooted in finite-element methods with a Galerkin formulation and offers superior conservation properties compared to conventional methods. Through finite-element analysis, it's proven that the method rigorously conserves key physical quantities, including energy and L2 norm, up to a level constrained by floating-point arithmetic precision. Demonstration of the method's efficacy is provided by presenting results from numerical tests and simulations of chaotic electron movements in high-energy plasas. These simulations confirm high accuracy and demonstrate the potential for long-term conservation of essential physical quantities when applied to intricate systems.

Simulating typical differential equations often requires adjusting the time step, and some equations even have math-proven issues when using fixed time steps. A series of highly accurate numerical methods have been created to address these times-typical equations, including both step-size fixed and variable timestep versions, with the latter yet to be fully developed and documented. This study focuses on developing and documenting a specific variable timestep method known as SD3IM, although similar techniques apply to other typical methods like SD2IM, SD4IM, and SD5IMs, which will be the subject of a subsequent paper.

In a Banach space, we have developed conditions for the existence and uniqueness of the solution to the Lyapunov equation when it involves bounded linear operators, and we've established a method for evaluating the well-posedness and stability of C0-semigroups in terms of this equation and its solution, particularly in cases where small perturbations occur in the operator, its inverse, or its solution to the Lyapunov equation.

To aid in the search for dimuonium at particle colliders, we have created MuMuPy, a practical tool. This software, available to download at https://github.com/jeanlouisvachon/MuMuPy, allows users to simulate dimuonium interactions with different materials. Using the electron-positron annihilation process, dimuonium's behavior within substances is examined. The results include the dimuonium's range within a material and its optical properties, specifically the energy-dependent refractive index and absorptive coefficient. Notably, for dimensions exceeding the dimuonium pair mean free path, dimuonium's effect on a material's opacity becomes a crucial consideration in experimental setups.

This research paper examines the optimal investment strategy for a pension fund, measuring its wealth relative to that of a reference fund. We focus on the geometric average of the ratio of wealth to that of the reference fund. By applying a power utility function to this measure, we can generalize a result from Andrei Barndorff-Nielsen et al. (2018), which concerned a risk-minimizing investment with a similar reference ratio. We derive a closed-form solution for the optimal strategy and investigate its properties in relation to the parameters of the power utility function. When the parameters indicate a risk-averse or risk-neutral stance, it's optimal to invest such that wealth never falls below zero; conversely, we identify under which parameters a universal constant allocation is optimal.

We have created the DIMOGAT galaxy catalogue, a dataset of 100 faint galaxies,
comprising a and b type densovirus, with redshifts under 0.05, to study their
intergalactic medium properties. These faint galaxies, dimmer than 28 Baryonic
magnitude at our redshift, are ideal for examining their circumgalactic and
intergalactic medium properties. Using Hubble Space Telescope observations, we
studied their circumgalactic and intergalactic medium properties. Our analysis
revealed that many of these galaxies lack bright central bulges, allowing us to
explore their intergalactic medium properties. This is the first study to
examine the intergalactic medium of galaxies at low redshifts.

A weakly interacting Berezinskii-Sutherland-Teller-Langer soliton is used to model local bosons, which are then coupled to fermionic quasiparticles via a contact interaction. The system is examined at the very limit of an extremely large potential well, which reveals a sudden and abrupt change in how the fermions interact with the bosons, leading to a more complex understanding of phase shifts at the extremely large potential well, known as an S-wave limit. Unlike the typical high-energy limit where fermions no longer interact with bosons, the system here undergoes a more complex collapse, which is linked to a specific complex pole in the t-matrix, accompanied by a imaginary component in the momentum transfer that doesn't occur at the B-S-T-L soliton. Instead of a gradual increase in the number of bound states, which typically occurs when linking local bosons to fermions, the system here undergoes a more complex collapse, losing two bound states when it is more strongly coupled. The research also explores the effects of an s-pole in the t-matrix, which causes a more complex collapse behavior, and how the system reacts to the local bosons, leading to a more complex increase in the number of bound states, which is not typically seen in the system, and how the system reacts to the local bosons, leading to a more complex increase in the number of bound states, which is not typically seen in the system.

This paper examines the average length of words representing non-trivial elements in the generalized Thompson groups $G_n$ and their counterparts in higher symmetry and braid Thompson groups, with a focus on near optimal thresholds for this average length in the standard generating sets. It also explores the divergence of non-trivial elements in the infinite braided Thompson group $\mathcal{G}_\infty$, including its average length of words, and establishes theories to analyze this divergence, leveraging concepts such as tree representation, bijection preservation, and partial maps on trees.

This paper enhances the recently developed Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework (including the DPR seeker) to improve its performance in handling inquiry-response tasks. Several key refinements have been made to the framework, including a modified attention mechanism for context-aware generation and a refined loss function for better generation. Experimental results confirm the effectiveness of these refinements and highlight the need for improvements in the RAG framework. Our changes to the framework remain open-source for future development and collaboration.

This research investigates a specific scenario in asymptotic analysis, where inferences about the large-behavior of orthogonal polynomials $\pi_{n}$ are made in a circumstance that is logarilymically more complex than the standard case. The standard case is characterized by the weight function $\omega(x)$, defined on the interval $(-1,1)$, which remains bounded and satisfies the condition $\omega(x) > 0$ almost everywhere. The researchers derive an explicit formula for the asymptotic expression of $\pi_{n}(x)$, derived from the Riemann-Hilbert problem, which is associated with the weight function $\omega(x)$. The study's key finding is that $\pi_{n}(x)$ behaves similarly to a Hahn-Edwards type equation, which is characterized by the weight function $\tilde{\omega}(x)$, defined as $\tilde{\omega}(x) = |x-a|^{\alpha} |x-b|^{\beta} \omega(x)$, where $a$ and $b$ are points within the interval $(-1,1)$, and $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are positive numbers less than or equal to $1$.

Human annotators play a crucial role in assessing the outputs generated by Machine Translation systems to ensure quality control.
When selecting annotators, it's essential to choose individuals with specific expertise, such as a background in a particular domain or proficiency in a relevant language.
We investigate the process of identifying such qualified annotators on the Amazon Mechanical Turk platform, where we attempt to find individuals who match our specific criteria within a larger population of workers.
We analyze the difficulty of locating these individuals in comparison to an average worker, and in doing so, we create a new metric called the 'needle score' to quantify this difficulty.
This metric is calculated by measuring how often our target keywords appear in the profiles of the available workers, with a higher score indicating a more challenging search.
We provide a detailed description of the 'needle scores' associated with various search criteria, including but not limited to, professional skills and language proficiency.
We discover that workers with particular characteristics, such as a bachelor's degree or fluency in German, are more likely to self-identify as having these attributes, making them easier to identify within the MTurk worker population.
Furthermore, we find that workers with a history of high-quality annotations also self-report a variety of other traits.
We conclude by discussing the implications of our findings and offer some practical advice for effectively searching for and recruiting qualified annotators on the MTurk platform.

Text-text and video-text retrieval have been relatively well studied, but text-video retrieval remains a more challenging task due to the temporal aspects involved. Existing methods often rely heavily on Recurrent Neural Networks or Transformer models, but these approaches can be limited in their capacity to capture vital video semantics or effectively attend to significant temporal regions. To address this issue, we propose TS2-Net, a Transformer model incorporating two key modules: a Token Shift module and a Token Selection module. The Token Shift module aims to capture local video dynamics by simulating Recurrent Neural Network behavior, while the Token Selection module pinpoints and aggregates global temporal information. Through thorough experiments, TS2-Net has demonstrated superior performance in both zero-shot and standard text-text and video-text retrieval tasks, achieving particularly impressive results with third-party datasets. Furthermore, TS2-Net has shown promising results when applied to YouTube8M, a large-scale video sentiment analysis dataset.

The significant mass of the top quark offers the potential for new weak neutral currents that could be unique to the top quark domain. These novel neutral currents, which modify the top quark's interactions at high energies, could manifest through a distinct missing energy signature at the LHC, paired with a top quark and potentially a large transverse momentum. The introduction of a new color-octet scalar boson in left-right symmetric models, which incorporate additional gauge bosons, provides a concrete realization of these novel neutral currents. The presence of this scalar boson at the LHC is anticipated to be detectable, which in turn would trigger re-evaluation of the top quark's neutral current couplings, a reassessment that is justified by the need to ensure unitarity. The interplay between this scalar boson's production and decay processes offers compelling evidence for these novel neutral currents, which become increasingly evident as data from the LHC's high-luminosity runs accumulate. The associated signals' increasing visibility, characterized by elevated rates and reduced background interference, will provide increasingly clear indications of these novel neutral currents in future datasets.

In directed hybrid random graphs, preference of connection is given based on existing weight when linking nodes, which are initially unconnected. When nodes are linked, a certain number of weights are randomly distributed. To investigate the effects of node weighting and link randomness, researchers compared the resulting networks against those generated using a uniform linking method, where all nodes have equal connection probability regardless of existing weight. Through simulations and calculations, researchers found that both models exhibit power-law degree distribution and clustering, but the distribution ranges show inverse relationships with respect to random weight parameters.

A network analyzer is a crucial component in maintaining the smooth functioning of commercial wireless communication systems, tasked with identifying disruptive devices such as network infrastructure, multilabel wireless disturbances, and illegal unauthorized networks. Recent research has focused on developing machine learning-based methods to identify these disruptive devices in wireless environments. However, current approaches tend to be overly dependent on signal strength data and struggle with class imbalance issues. To address these challenges, we have developed an innovative machine learning model, the Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), which leverages the spatial characteristics of radio signals. By normalizing and aligning the spatial features of radio signals, our method utilizes a CNN to classify convolutional layers, effectively identifying large and small interfering devices. To mitigate class imbalance, we have applied the Focal Loss function, which enhances the model's ability to accurately detect small interfering devices, ultimately improving overall performance, as evidenced by experiments conducted on the CEM-2018 dataset.

A novel spacetime model, known as the Som-Raychaudhuri cosmic string spacetime, has been suggested to describe the environment around localized mass distributions. Our study builds a non-inertial spacetime based on the Som-Raychaudhuri model, and we analyze entities satisfying the Klein-Gordon equation in this spacetime. By separating variables in the Klein-Gordon equation using a specific coordinate system with specific constraints, we obtain a separable form with a specific spectrum equation. We also establish relationships between energy and vorticity, as well as between energy and electric charge, in our analysis. Additionally, we verify the non-negative property of the vorticity. By comparing the obtained spectrum equation to the Schrödinger equation, we establish a specific correspondence. We validate our results through three-dimensional visualizations of the Vortensity map and a 3D plot of the radial wave function slice at specific values.

A measure algebra is considered typical at a specified measure if, for any given tolerance and any measure-bounding function, there exists a positive threshold such that, for any measure below the threshold, the measure-bounded function, and a measure exceeding the threshold, a specific transformation yields nearly equivalent results for a specific function value, with a negligible difference in the resulting probability of another set, this negligible quantity tending to zero as the threshold tends to zero. Similarly, there is an equivalent characterization characteristic of Bochner algebras. Moreover, there is an equivalent characterization characteristic of the algebra of essentially bounded essentially bounded functions of a measure space.

We have studied the polarization of the proton and its role in the double parton distribution process, focusing on the deep virtual Compton scattering process. When the proton is prepared in a polarized state, new observables become accessible that are not dependent on target spin. Assuming quark-gluon symmetry in the proton's frame, we have derived the underlying coefficients of this phenomenon, revealing an important distinction between the electron-proton and proton-proton reactions, particularly in the $T20$ structure function where the proton-gluon interaction is enucleated.

This research proposes a definition of Artificial Intelligence enhanced by data, leading to the concept of Enhanced Artificial Intelligence. This enhancement enables the seamless transformation of traditional AI modules more complex than basic computational units into statistical models, thereby allowing a comprehensive re-examination of established AI frameworks. Based on this perspective, we present a theoretical framework that mathematically describes enhanced AI systems and provides a formal structure for data-driven improvement. We also establish various principles for data integration that can be used to develop different algorithms, which are subsequently formalized and illustrated with three examples: enhanced artificial chess players, autonomous vehicle navigation, and real-time traffic management.

Our research focuses on the thermal properties of a bosonic system, comprised of spin-orbit linked particles in a periodic lattice with multiple and time-varying fluorescence frequencies, subjected to thermal fluctuations within the non-degenerate regime of the photonic field. We develop a comprehensive analytical model to derive the thermal modification of the superfluid's critical temperature, incorporating photonic effects. Our analytical and numerical results demonstrate a superlinear relationship between shifting superfluid critical temperature and fluorescence frequency in this thermal condition, resulting in an increased critical temperature with increased fluorescence frequency. Additionally, the phase diagram of the superfluid-modulated system exhibits a phenomenon where the superfluid phase boundary transitions from sinusoidal to nearly parabolic.

Graph theory concepts, specifically isomorphism and edge isomorphism of graphs, are connected to abelian groups through a certain type of matrix-valued edge weight framework. By imposing a maximal rank condition, it's possible to eliminate degeneracies in graphs defined by group characters. However, this method has a limitation as it's overly restrictive, often resulting in empty sets for the relevant parameters. Instead, a more relaxed maximal dependence condition can be applied, which allows for non-degenerate graphs to be defined with complex weights and, consequently, leads to criteria for isomorphism and edge isomorphism in terms of abelian groups. Furthermore, this method is used to establish a correspondence between graph hierarchies and the chains of subgroups within a group.

We have derived new results in two and three dimensional extensions of the AdS/CFT correspondence, resulting from compactifications of the type IIA theory, involving D2 and D3 branes. In three dimensional adS$_4$, the dual fields in the large N, large 't Hooft coupling limit exhibit integer and half-integer spins with positively real scaling dimensions, which is possible due to the existence of supersymmetric dual pairs of chiral multiplets and supercharges in the boundary conformal field theory. These results arise as a consequence of the compactifications of the ten dimensional theory, as supported by solutions to the bulk fields' equations of motion.

Researchers have been developing novel kernel functions by analyzing Gaussian Processes through basic mathematical principles. This systematic approach allows for the creation of new Gaussian Process kernels that maintain mathematical coherence and geometric consistency within the GRF framework. Four distinct Gaussian Process kernels were introduced in our framework, and their performance was rigorously evaluated using benchmark datasets in both classification and regression tasks. The empirical findings demonstrate that the proposed methods exhibit performance comparable to, and in some cases exceeding, established state-of-the-art Gaussian Process Gaussian Mixture Model (GPGMM) and Gaussian Process Classifier (GPC) approaches. Furthermore, the integration of the new kernels into GRFs enhances the accuracy of Gaussian Process Gaussian Mixture Cluster (GPGMC) and Gaussian Process Based Clustering (GPBC) methods.

The development of a high-luminosity muon collider requires the creation of
beam-beam instabilities mitigation strategies to mitigate the detrimental effects
of neutral beam debris produced by beam-plasma interactions at the interaction
point. This paper aims to investigate muon bundle motion within the debris
formation region to determine its impact on the muon beam's properties. 
Specifically, this paper explores ways to reduce the detrimental effects of
beam debris on muon beam parameters through careful management of the beam's
current distribution and beam separation. The results of this analysis provide a
set of guidelines for the design of muon colliders in the next generation.

We propose a novel set of regularly constrained loss functions for feature differentiability, facilitating both structured and continuous sparsity promotion. Regulated loss functions employ optimal transport theory to guide probability distributions towards target shapes. The introduction of geometric constraints on joint distributions enables the promotion of various forms of sparsity. By contrast to existing methods, which rely on existing distributions for gradients, joint distributions in our approach are jointly optimized with model weights. Experimental results demonstrate that our regulated losses yield superior performance in comparison to existing sparse learning techniques.

The unique properties of superfluid $^3$He have garnered significant attention, particularly in certain thin films where multiple odd-parity states can interact due to weak inhomogeneity. In this film type, one specific state can exhibit a unique behavior where it is effectively blocked from interacting with others, a phenomenon that can be observed in the absence of a magnetic field. This phenomenon is known as the Pauli obstruction and is typically associated with systems having fermionic statistics. A recent study has demonstrated that a similar Pauli obstruction can emerge in superfluid systems with bosonic statistics, specifically in certain weakly interacting Bose fluids confined to geometries with tunable dispersion relations. This study has identified two conditions that enable the emergence of this phenomenon, including a situation where a specific type of correlation function is minimized. This novel discovery could pave the way for developing new superfluid systems that can be used for quantum information processing and other applications.

To maintain software test quality, it's crucial to be aware of test odors, which are distinct from general software smells as they specifically affect testing quality. To identify significant test odors, researchers employed a mixed research approach, starting with an exhaustive literature review, followed by a structured interview process with test developers to determine their perspectives on notable test odors. Through a systematic analysis of the data, researchers categorized 21 test odors, with 10 classified as severe based on their potential consequences, frequency, and impact on software quality of life.

Given a nonconvex, lower-continuous function of two variables with an uncountably large domain, we initially reformulate a sweeping procedure as a integro-differential equation involving a mixed derivative. This equation, under certain growth and smoothness conditions, ensures the existence and uniqueness of weak solutions, which, in turn, are demonstrated to be the generalised value it-erations of corresponding dynamic programming equations. Consequently, the theoretical findings provide the justification of generalised value it-erations and a novel, computation-efficient algorithm for solving nonconvex Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equations.

The `kkmcee` software, a multi-photon Monte Carlo event creator for lepton colliders, is introduced. The tool is designed to generate Monte Carlo events for lepton colliders with multi-photon corrections up to four photons. It includes calculations for initial state radiation (ISR), final state radiation (FSR), multiple soft photons, beaming effects, resonance scanning, Boson Ghost Sum Rules, form factors, and more. The program is further equipped with utilities for generating event lists, running fits, and creating custom Monte Carlo event samples. The mounting effects on the $e^+e^-$ cross section are illustrated with event samples for the Z boson, Higgs boson, and a heavy quark, demonstrating the Z boson cross section reduction of a factor of 3.9 due to these effects at a center of mass energy of 91.18 GeV.

Determining the inter-beat interval through the analysis of beat onsets in signals underpinns the creation of various vital signs indicators essential for the assessment of cardio-respiratory health, but the process is typically plagued by numerous errors resulting from error propagation. The potential ramifications of such inaccuracies are significant given that clinical decisions are often based on the calculated metrics. The issue can be addressed through direct estimation of the interval, however, the majority of the currently available methods rely on postprocessing, which is less efficient and less accurate. The novel approach introduced below involves the adaptation of the Tiramisu framework, originally designed for signal denoising purposes, in order to minimize interval error propagation and eliminate postprocessing. In order to test the efficacy of this approach, it has been implemented on synthetic inter-beat interval and heartbeat signals, as well as real clinical ECG data, and experimental results demonstrate its superiority over traditional postprocessing techniques in terms of significantly reduced interval error propagation. Furthermore, it has been observed that decision-making based on the inter-beat interval is significantly more accurate with this approach compared to traditional postprocessing methods.

This study introduces Stochastical SVD, a new randomization-based method for low-rank factorization of tensors. SVD is derived from an extension of the iterative stochastic algorithm used in matrix factorization, which converges even with multiple passes over the data. The method draws灵感 from previous tensor decomposition approaches, sharing similarities with power iteration, alternating least squares, and stochastic gradient descent techniques. We demonstrate that our algorithm retains the benefits of randomness, specifically efficiency and robustness, while offering distinct advantages over existing methods.

As graphs represent the progression of real-world scenarios, there's a growing need for methods to dynamically capture and capture these changes. Existing techniques primarily focus on graph static analysis, there's a knowledge gap in the area of graph dynamic analysis. This paper presents an approach to a fundamental problem in graph dynamic analysis: one-step embedding of evolving graphs. As this task is computationally demanding, we propose a problem definition that involves using task-specific features to provide a more compact representation of the graph. Our approach focuses on developing dynamic graph neural networks to embed evolving graphs. Building upon this definition, we conducted an extensive benchmark study of six methods on three comprehensive datasets. Based on these results, we propose two novel networks, E-EE and E-EE+, that outperform the benchmark methods.

Our study examines the hydrogen-photon induced reaction with tritium, focusing on the intermediate state of $^7$H. By analyzing the reaction cross sections, we determined the mass of the $^7$H resonance to be 6.6506(5) MeV/c$^2$, above the nucleon threshold, with a breadth of 1.360(5) MeV. To investigate the structure of $^7$H, we used the Skyrme force and compared the calculated wave functions with those of $^7$Li, which shares the same nucleon composition but differs in neutron arrangement. Our calculations suggest that $^7$H wave functions exhibit the characteristics of a three-body system consisting of $^3$H and two additional neutrons. Furthermore, the reaction mechanism of $^7$H was analyzed using the R-matrix theory, which revealed that the reactions $^7$H+$^{12}$C$\rightarrow$ $^8$n+$^{11}$C and $^7$H+$^{12}$C$\rightarrow$ 4n+$^{11}$B are dominated by electric dipole transitions.

This research paper examines the Dirichlet - nibremberg problem on the upper half spheres, where we investigate the existence of solutions for the problem expression I_a(lamda), a variation of its maximum value, a-lamda is the problem's best constant and lamda is a real number source term. A research paper is presented to show the problem's solutions exist under the condition that n is at least 5 and a falls within the open interval (0,1), with solutions exhibiting blow-up behavior at the boundary of the problem's domain, a unique and previously unexplored phenomenon for this problem, a variation of the nirenberg issue.

Recent advancements in deep representation learning have shown significant success,
with various approaches attempting to bridge the gap between complex data and
their underlying optimal transport representations. One such method, the
OPM-OT model, directly learns a deep network that minimizes the Wasserstein-2
distance between paired input-output samples. Unfortunately, this method often
struggles to reach convergence, resulting in suboptimal performance compared
to conventional deep learning models. Our research proposes the DR-OT model,
which builds upon the OPM-OT approach and leverages the Sinkhorn distances to
improve both model performance and optimization efficiency. The DR-OT model uses
a multi-objective framework to optimize distinct layers, effectively separating
transport and non-transport components and reducing convergence barriers.
Through rigorous experimentation, the DR-OT model achieves notable gains in
classification and regression tasks, with insights into its behavior and limits
also gained.

We've developed a mathematical framework to simulate the impact of regional tracing collaborations in the UK's contact tracing system. The model indicates that the regional barriers result in an estimated 20-30% decrease in contacts traced, despite national efforts to improve tracing efficiency. By harmonizing the tracing efficiency across all UK regions, we can optimize the amount of contacts traced.

Based on the extended V and B-V photometry from 2MASS, a catalog of Melotte 72 open cluster members has been created using Gaia DR2 astrometry. An analysis of Melotte 72's properties, including position, age, and characteristics, has been carried out using photometric data from various sources. Utilizing isochrone fitting, a consistent cluster age of approximately 3.6 billion years has been determined. Our cluster mass determination yields a value close to 2000 solar masses. Our cluster distance modulus assessment yields a value of approximately 8.04 mag. Calculations reveal the cluster's parallax to be 0.127 mas, translating to a distance of approximately 7.86 kpc. Calculations show the cluster's logarithmic metallicity ratio to be close to zero. Our cluster kinematic analysis reveals it to be moving towards the Galactic center. Our cluster vertical velocity is estimated to be approximately 14.7 km/s. Our velocity dispersion along the line of sight is estimated to be approximately 2.1 km/s. Our velocity dispersion perpendicular to the line of sight is estimated to be approximately 21.7 km/s. Our analysis shows Melotte 72 is a metal-poor cluster located in the Galactic disk, situated at a distance of approximately 2.5 kiloparsecs from the Galactic plane. Its membership status remains uncertain.

We investigate the average complexity of a specific algebraic problem by analyzing the growth pattern of a sequence of randomly generated polynomials. Building upon a proposed model of sparse complex polynomial systems, we investigate the average characteristics of these systems, which are defined over parameters from the standard standard normal distribution. Based on numerical experiments conducted with small-scale systems, we observe a consistent pattern where the average complexity increases at a rate proportional to the square root of the system's dimension, a result supported by recent research findings, which reveals an average complexity increase rate of $\sqrt{2}/2$ for two-variable Gaussian polynomials.

This research focuses on leveraging unsupervised image-based self-calibration to model the intrinsic parameters of a single eye-in-hand pinhole camera. Since pinhole cameras cannot physically be reoriented, our proposed framework modelss parallax observations by simulating camera rotations. All model parameters are optimized in a fully data-driven sequence, which necessitates the incorporation of both cyclic and non-cyclic rotation sequences. To facilitate efficient parameter estimation, our framework also employs an image rendering technique utilizing OpenCV's pre-computed hardware-accelerated lookup tables for rapidly computed DCT-based pixel transformations. Experimental outcomes are demonstrated on both artificially created and real-world datasets, showcasing our model's capabilities.

A comprehensive, formal model of restricted MDPs, encompassing inverse reinforcement learning and policy learning, is developed on the basis of partially observed restricted MFDPs that are projected into observable forms, with a new issue of restricted inverse reinforcement learning being identified as a crucial sub-task. This model leads to both a formulation of the issue and an algorithm - ORRF, a principled approach for learning a restricted model from data and an optimal policy. Our research includes a detailed analysis of the data requirements, the impact of model mismatches, and the efficiency of our algorithm, supported by empirical evaluations on several continuous control tasks.

The European Space Agency's Astrophysics program has selected the Galactic Mapping Mission, known as GAIA, as its priority for a medium-class all-sky mission to undertake in the early 2010s.  This ambitious undertaking, led by a European team, employs the concept of a virtual observatory to extract data from diverse, existing all-sky missions, including the release of the dataset by the KMTNet collaboration.  This unique integration allows GAIA to focus on a specific area of the sky, where KMTNet has observed a gas cloud, known as the "Lemon Cloud."
